planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; give Pink-A-Boo room to reach its full arching spread rather than crowding it against other shrubs.

directions: This Monrovia-introduced hybrid deutzia produces dense, pendulous clusters of star-shaped flowers that shade from deep pink at the petal base to pale pink and white at the margins, opening in late spring and covering the arching branches for about two weeks. The bushy, upright-arching habit reaches well above eye level at maturity, larger than most garden deutzia, and works best as a specimen, informal hedge, or background shrub with room to spread. Bright green lance-shaped leaves turn burgundy in autumn, adding a second season of interest after bloom. Prune lightly right after flowering to shape and remove old wood, since flower buds form on the previous year's growth.

common_name: Perle Rose Deutzia (Lemoine Frosted-Edge Pink Hybrid Deutzia)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in average to fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Perle Rose tolerates dry, mediocre soils once established but blooms best with reliable moisture.

directions: Bred by the Lemoine nursery from Deutzia longifolia and D. discolor, this hybrid produces long sprays of star-shaped flowers in a sustained rose pink shading to a frosty white edge on each petal, opening later in the season than many deutzia and drawing bees while lightly scenting the air. The bushy, multi-stemmed shrub keeps a rounded, upright form and holds up well against disease and pests, tolerating average or dry soils without fuss. Light green spring foliage matures to a deeper green that sets off the pink flower clusters and later provides a backdrop for summer perennials. Renew by thinning out the oldest canes right after flowering to keep the shrub from becoming congested.

common_name: Waterton Mock Orange (Cold-Hardy Alberta Lewis's Mock Orange)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Waterton is among the hardiest mock oranges and tolerates a wide range of soils and exposures once established.

directions: Selected at the Alberta Horticultural Research Station from native Lewis's mock orange stock, Waterton is prized as the hardiest named mock orange, shrugging off prairie winters that would damage most other cultivars. Clusters of sweetly fragrant white flowers cover the upright, spreading branches in early summer, followed by green foliage that turns yellow in fall. Its rugged constitution and adaptability to poor or variable soils make it a dependable choice for hedges, screens, or background plantings in cold-winter regions. Prune immediately after flowering to control size, since Waterton naturally forms a large, multi-stemmed thicket if left unchecked.

common_name: Blizzard Mock Orange (Morden Pure-White Lewis's Mock Orange)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Blizzard is drought tolerant once established and needs little supplemental water beyond its first season.

directions: Selected from a seedling population in Alberta and released by the Morden Research Station, Blizzard produces loose clusters of large, two-inch pure white flowers with soft yellow stamens and a strong, sweet fragrance reminiscent of orange and pineapple. Bloom is so profuse in early summer that the rounded to vase-shaped shrub appears blanketed in white, giving the cultivar its name. Once established it tolerates drought and a range of soils, making it a low-maintenance choice for a sunny border, screen, or pollinator planting. Thin out a portion of the oldest stems after flowering each year to keep the shrub vigorous and well shaped.

common_name: Starbright Mock Orange (Newfoundland Sterile Fragrant Mock Orange)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist but well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Starbright is unusually cold hardy for a mock orange and is a good choice where other cultivars struggle to overwinter.

directions: Developed at the Memorial University Botanical Garden in Newfoundland, Starbright was bred in part for extra cold hardiness and bears large, pure white, intensely fragrant flowers with dark purplish-black calyces that make the opening buds look like tiny stars. Dark purplish young stems and bronzy-purple new foliage maturing to dark green give the shrub interest even between bloom flushes. Because the flowers are sterile, Starbright puts its energy into a long, showy bloom period in early summer rather than seed production. Grow it as an upright specimen or informal hedge, pruning immediately after flowering to maintain shape and encourage strong new growth.

common_name: Snow Dwarf Mock Orange (Compact Double-Flowered Dwarf Mock Orange)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Snow Dwarf's compact size suits foundation plantings and small gardens where full-size mock orange would be too large.

directions: This dwarf hybrid mock orange forms a dense, rounded, multi-stemmed mound only two to three feet tall, far smaller than most Philadelphus, making it useful where a full-size shrub would overwhelm the space. Fragrant, double white flowers to about an inch and a half across cluster loosely at the branch tips in late spring, standing out against dark green, finely serrated foliage that holds its color through the season without notable fall change. It grows quickly under average garden conditions and tolerates a range of soils as long as it does not dry out completely. Prune only after flowering to avoid removing next year's buds, since bloom occurs on the previous season's wood.

common_name: Bowles's Variety Mock Orange (Cream-Margined Variegated Sweet Mock Orange)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; some afternoon shade helps prevent leaf scorch on the cream-margined foliage in hot climates.

directions: An RHS Award of Garden Merit selection named for English gardener E. A. Bowles, this variegated mock orange bears medium green leaves broadly edged in creamy white, giving the compact, rounded shrub year-round texture even before it flowers. Strongly scented, creamy-white blooms about an inch across open in early summer among the variegated foliage, echoing the leaf margins. The shrub keeps a tidier, more rounded outline than the species and works well as a bright accent in a mixed border or woodland edge where its foliage contrast can be appreciated after bloom fades. Renewal-prune older stems right after flowering to keep variegation fresh and prevent the shrub from becoming leggy.
